entry.title: Earhart Expedition: The Search Continues After Taraia Object Investigation Rules Out Hypothesis

media:group.media:title: Earhart Expedition: The Search Continues After Taraia Object Investigation Rules Out Hypothesis
media:group.media:description:
The Taraia Object expedition, a joint effort by the Archaeological Legacy Institute, Purdue Research Foundation and Purdue University, found no conclusive evidence to confirm a hypothesis that wreckage from Amelia Earhart’s Lockheed Electra 10-E was in a lagoon on a remote atoll in the South Pacific.
The findings mark a new chapter in the ongoing effort to understand what happened to Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan on her round-the-world flight attempt in 1937.
While the findings rule out one of the latest hypotheses, they also provide valuable information that will help inform future efforts to solve one of aviation’s greatest mysteries.
“Amelia Earhart never gave up — she kept pushing boundaries and flying into the unknown,” said Steve Schultz, Purdue’s general counsel and member of the expedition. “That same fire fuels our search. She kept flying, and we will keep searching.”
Purdue’s connection to Earhart remains a powerful part of the university’s history, and the commitment to pursuing answers continues.
Get the latest update: https://www.purdue.edu/newsroom/2026/Q4/search-for-amelia-earharts-plane-continues-after-taraia-object-expedition-on-nikumaroro-rules-out-latest-hypothesis

media:group.media:title: Earhart Expedition: Back to Work
media:group.media:description:
After several days of rough seas and strong winds, the weather has finally cleared, and the expedition team is heading back to the lagoon on Nikumaroro.
Once there, they will quickly get to work on the second of three planned phases in investigating the Taraia Object to determine if it is Amelia Earhart’s missing plane.
